LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the house know that Her Royal Highness Princess Elizabeth is celebrating today her twenty-first birthday. His Excellency the Governor General has sent a message of congratulations and best wishes to her Royal Highness, and I am sure it will be the wish of all hon. members to have it noted on Hansard today that the House of Commons desires to be associated in the closest possible manner with the expression of these congratulations and good wishes.",,,,

On behalf of this party I want to associate myself with what he had to say.

Mr. M. J. COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar); Mr. Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister has expressed I think the views of every member of the house, and we in this party wish to be associated with this expression of congratulations.

Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, speaking for this group I am sure that the Acting Prime Minister has expressed the wishes of the whole house, and we wish to be associated with what he has said.

CHURCH (Broadview):,,PRINCESS ELIZABETH,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,SECOND REPORT REFERRED BACK,"Mr. Speaker, the report should be sent back to the committee for further consideration. The time has gone by when we should be sending abroad these missionary committees which amount to nothing. All the information on Palestine and UNO can be found in the library, but members are not studious enough to go into the library and learn something about the united nations, which is a failure. If the United States and Great Britain cannot solve the complicated Palestine question coming before the united nations, nobody can. The Palestine question is a very complicated one and is made more so by the presence of

Jews in Germany as well as in Palestine. On the other hand the Arabs, who are very powerful, have aided Britain and have supporters in every country. We are spending money like water on these useless missions like the UNO all over the seven seas. I object to this report being adopted. It should be sent back to the committee.
Amendment (Mr. St. Laurent) agreed to.

column2: Other than three periodicals published by the Department of National Health and Welfare, all health education material such as books, pamphlets, folders and posters is produced) in quantity at the federal level and shipped in bulk to provincial departments where it is used by public health nurses and others in closest contact with the public. Quantities for all V.D. literature are determined by the provinces and then shipped to them after printing. This is in accordance with a recommendation made by the Dominion Council of Health.

column1: In addition a great many individual requests are received and filled1 by this department for such publications as ""The Canadian Mother and Child"". Such requests come from expectant mothers, doctors, public health nurses and others in that field of endeavour. Further, many requests for informational material are received from groups and organizations such as the Women's Institutes, Red Cross, Home and School Associations and others. The department makes every effort to fill such requests as received.

column1: This bulletin is designed as a clearing house for health and welfare information between federal, provincial and municipal departments and independent and voluntary health, welfare and social service organizations. It seeks to publicize nation-wide health and welfare policies and problems, to acquaint each province and municipality with advances in other provinces and municipalities and to instil in medical, public health, welfare and community leaders a greater appreciation of health and welfare, services. It is distributed to all doctors, dentists, public health workers, social service and welfare workers, nurses, legislators both federal and provincial, teachers, municipal officials, clergy, trade unions, service clubs, women's organizations, libraries, newspapers, radio stations, and to many private citizens who request copies. The circulation list is, in common with other departmental periodicals, under constant revision.

1463054,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.2.11.2,1947-04-21,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,,Minister of National Health and Welfare,QUESTIONS,MERCHANT SEAMEN-MEDICAL CARE,,1.
column2: (a) Such medical, surgical or other treatment as the case requires is provided under authority of Part V of the Canada Shipping Act.
Grants are made annually to twelve institutions assisting sailors, in eight of the chief ports, namely Halifax, Sydney, North Sydney, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal, Vancouver and Victoria.

Under authority of order in council P.C. 1862 of March 24, 1941, maintenance and medical care are provided for non-resident seamen who, because of mental or physical disabilities, were left in Canada during the war and whom it has not yet been possible to return to their own countries.

column2: Has the attention of the government been called to an address by the Rt. Hon. Viscount Bennett, former prime minister of Canada to the Women's Advertising Club in London, England, on April 15, that ""Britain could no longer defend the commonwealth of nations?""

MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance,AVAILABILITY OF SUPPLIES IN BRITISH COLUMBIA,,,I think the remark that most often met British Columbia members when they went home at Easter was the supply of butter for British Columbia. Members from that province have pretty well all taken part in asking for some information; therefore I am pleased to answer now the question just asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo.

The situation throughout British Columbia has been very difficult in recent weeks. There are several factors which have a bearing, among the most important being a tendency to store butter in expectation of realizing a profit when the present eight and a half cents per pound government subsidy is withdrawn by May 1. Announcement by the government on March 19 that the government will insist upon a full recovery of inventory profits after the subsidy is discontinued has helped the situation but has not overcome it altogether. A second important factor in the shortage has been slowing down of shipments from the prairie provinces. The administrative officials have been taking all steps available to keep the British Columbia market supplied with butter and are continuing to put forth every effort in this regard. Since January, 1947, all butter offered in Saskatchewan and Alberta has been moved into British Columbia and no shipments have moved into the eastern provinces since that date. Last week four carloads of butter were directed to British Columbia from Saskatchewan. In addition a supply of 8,000 boxes, or 450,000 pounds, of imported butter has been transported across Canada from the east coast into British Columbia.

According to Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures on butter storage as at April 1, 1947, stocks of butter in storage in all parts of Canada are somewhat higher than at the same date last year. Even British Columbia has somewhat more butter in storage than one year ago. It is however, as you can imagine, extremely difficult to divert and

order out supplies which are held by a very large number of operators, not only large packers but also retailers, restaurants, hotels and so on. The situation in eastern Canada is undoubtedly better than in British Columbia but, as I have stated, the costs of transporting butter from the east to the west is one important factor against doing so.

1463126,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.13.1.7,1947-04-21,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,EMERGENCY POWERS,CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS,,Mr. Chairman, I made a short statement on this subject on Friday night.
Emergency Powers

This is a situation which concerns the Department of Reconstruction, for the reason that, by cooperation with the cities and municipalities, the Wartime Housing and Mortgage Company so far has been able to make it possible to keep a roof over the heads of Canadian citizens. I am exceedingly anxious that we shall continue to do so. The hon. member for Eglinton has moved an amendment to the wartime leasehold regulations whereby a veteran may secure possession of any house owned by him. No one in this house would deny that such a step is desirable if circumstances permit. The argument against this amendment is exactly the same as the argument for retaining eviction control generally. Throughout the country there is acute housing congestion, and the housing requirements are being met only by a very large amount of involuntary multiple occupancy.

I think it is fair to say that a large part of the multiple occupancy is that of the veteran and his family living with their in-laws. The exact size of this multiple occupancy is difficult to determine, but from sample surveys it would appear that there was multiple occupancy ranging from ten to twenty per cent, depending upon the municipality. There is a general impression that congestion is largely in the metropolitan areas. That is not correct. In many instances the multiple occupancy is much heavier in municipalities of 5,000 to 15,000 than it is in Toronto and Montreal.

For instance, in August 1946 it was found that in Carleton Place there were 1,100 families and only 900 residential units in which to house these families. This means that in Carleton Place there were 200 individual units housing more than one family, and about 400 families living in multiple occupancy. Another case in point is Smith's Falls, where in September 1946 there were 2,700 families and 1,946 housing units.

Under the present wartime leasehold regulations there are circumstances under which an owner may secure possession of a house owned by him. Experience has shown that where permits or orders are given for possession, there is a net loss of living accommodation. The extreme case is an owner living in multiple occupancy of rented premises who is given right of possession to a house owned by him which is also in multiple occupancy. The net effect of such a transaction is the loss of two units, because it is most unlikely that the residence which the owner leaves will go back into a state of multiple occupancy. In other words, the

owner of a house and his family will take in his son and daughter-in-law and their family, but if the son and daughter-in-law leave, it is most unlikely that the owner of the house will take another family into multiple occupancy. The two families dispossessed by the returning owner are in the market for two units, which under present conditions are not available. There are, of course, certain instances in which an owner, given the right of possession to the house he owns, leaves his residence to take possession of the owned premises where there also is a single tenant. It is estimated that under present conditions

column2: evictions involve the net loss of 750 units for this reason.

column1: In February, 1947, a change was made in the leasehold regulations, known as board order 688, whereby individuals who had purchased a house between October 31, 1944 and July 25, 1945, may secure possession on three months' notice provided that a court of rental appeals find that the need of the owner is greater than the need of the tenant. As at March 31 there were 1,433 applications 'received under order 688, hot including Alberta and Nova Scotia. The status of these applications as at March 31 was:

I have outlined these figures in detail because, although they are very much smaller in number than would be occasioned by the proposal of the hon. member for Eglinton, nevertheless the granting of these applications will place an additional burden upon our efforts with the municipalities to find space for evicted tenants.

To illustrate the situation I should like to give the hon. members figures for shelter needs in Ottawa. There are 484 units of emergency shelter in occupancy in Ottawa. There are 36 notices approved by the wartime prices and trade board to vacate self-contained units, most of which have effect on May 1. There are 57 notices approved by the wartime prices and trade board to vacate shared accommodation by May 1. In addition to these 93 cases of eviction, there are 74 families living in distressingly over-crowded or substandard conditions which are described by the emergency shelter administrator as being urgent cases. In addition to these 167 cases there have been 38 applications received under board order No. 688 to which I referred earlier. Applications have been granted in twelve cases, and there are fourteen more cases pending. To meet the needs of approxi-
Emergency Powers

mately 190 cases in all, the balance of available units in Rockcliffe, six in number, will be completed on May 1. We are at work on 120 emergency shelter units at Uplands to be completed by June 1. The potential of available shelter in all is 126 units.

Hon. members will see that even under the present restricted rights of owners to secure occupancy of residences owned by them and before any such amendment as now proposed, the municipalities are having difficulty in meeting present needs. I have used Ottawa as an example, but I can assure the hon. members that Ottawa is no more congested than the average municipality.

During the last eighteen months we have been working very closely with the city of Toronto along the same lines. There also we are coming to an end of buildings available for conversion. In greater Toronto there have been 417 applications received under order 688, of which 58 have been heard, 34 granted, 14 adjourned, 5 with reserved judgment, and 5 dismissed. We are not at all sure that even under the present regulations immediate needs for shelter in Toronto can be met.

It is to be remembered that the municipalities themselves are bearing the main burden of looking after families without accommodation. The dominion has been assisting the municipalities by making buildings available and by financial grants. Nevertheless the problem is one which must be faced by the municipalities. A change in the wartime leasehold regulations as now proposed will, in my opinion, make it impossible for the municipalities to meet increased needs. A chaotic situation would be created. I would remind hon. members of my statement of last Friday in which I pointed out that the supply of surplus buildings available for conversion into shelters is running very low. It is going to test our ingenuity to look after even present needs. I believe that such a step by the dominion at the present time would be most unfair to the municipalities. Some of our officials feel that even the increase occasioned by board order No. 688 has created a situation which may prove beyond capacity to meet. I will not attempt to estimate the number of evictions which might be caused by the proposal now before the house. I can assure the house, however, that the evictions resulting would be many times those occasioned by board order No. 688.

Hon. members must remember that in a condition of heavy multiple occupancy changes in tenancy result in a net loss of units. The housing situation is so tight that we cannot afford to lose units, and indeed

there may be no place for evicted families to go. No one denies that the rights of owners should be restored as quickly as possible. There is, however, a most extraordinary situation in the housing field, and at this time tlie most economical use of our short supply of housing must be weighed against the rights of the individual owner. The proposed amendment might create thousands of additional evictions at a time when the municipalities are putting forward their best efforts to deal with a very difficult situation. I firmly believe that any step which would increase the number of evictions at this time is against the public interest.

The government is making every effort to examine its orders in council in the light of criticism from the opposition. So far, in considering this measure in committee, changes have been made at the suggestion of the opposition which the government believed could be made with reasonable safety to the state. In the case under discussion I am convinced that the government would be derelict in its duty if it agreed to an amendment which in its opinion undoubtedly would have the effect of putting on the street families for whom no shelter can be made available. I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton would not wish to sponsor legislation which would have that effect. I would ask that he reexamine his proposed amendment in the light of the additional information I have just given, and consider withdrawing it.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1463127,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.13.1.8,1947-04-21,4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4,ca.m.9666,Mr. ABBOTT:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,EMERGENCY POWERS,CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS,,I wonder if I might add just a word. The committee will recall something of the history of rental control and of eviction control, and will remember that when the general freeze was put on in July, 1945, it was primarily to protect members of the armed forces and their families. Most of the troops were not then home, of course; at that time comparatively few had returned. It is also true that on their return a good many bought houses, but I thing we should remember that a great many returned veterans did not, and I am satisfied there are infinitely more veterans who are tenants than veterans who are owners of property.

As my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has pointed out, the fact is that there simply are not enough rental dwellings in Canada available for those who occupy that type of accommodation, and that is the problem we have to face. The rental administration, in view of the fact that there is a general freeze, has endeavoured to provide a reasonable and orderly way of seeing to it that those who now have a roof over their heads will continue to have such a roof, until
Emergency Powers

building has increased to the point where some relaxation of the eviction controls can be made. I am convinced that it would not be in the interests of the veterans themselves to provide now for a relaxation as suggested by the hon. member for Eglinton. Already some relief has been given under order 688 in regard to purchases made between November 1, 1944, and July 25, 1945, but as my colleague has pointed out that has resulted in a considerable number of applications for eviction, and some dislocation. I am satisfied that if an amendment were made now to the order, as suggested, it would result in veterans ousting veterans; and I think it is obvious that it would put a premium on the veteran who was in a financial position to purchase property as against the veteran who was not.
Taking all those factors into consideration it seems to me the government could not agree to an amendment to the rental order which would permit veteran owners being given this special protection.

Reference was made by my hon. friend to the control of shared accommodation. He seemed under the impression that there was no means of evicting tenants occupying this type of accommodation except by application to the court of rental appeals. Well, a large proportion of family units do live in shared accommodation. I am advised that something in the order of twenty to forty per cent of families in urban centres now live in rooms. All these people can be evicted on six months' notice. In view of the acute shortage of housing accommodation, it is felt that is the minimum length of notice which should be allowed. That is permitted under article 428 of the board, which permits the landlord to recover possession of such accommodation on six months' notice, which may be terminated at any time during the calendar year if he desires the accommodation as an extension of his own residence, but he is not bound to continue to occupy such accommodation for any specific period after recovery of possession.

I have always believed, personally, that these special rules which are made for veterans often defeat the very purpose for which they are set up. In the present instance I believe my hon. friend would agree that we would have to restrict it to veterans who had purchased their houses before a certain date. If you allowed it to continue in the future you would have a wild scramble for houses, and it obviously would break down. There would be discrimination at once between the veteran who had the financial means to purchase a house on a certain date and the man who would like to purchase one and

finds that he can do so now. But more serious is the fact that you still have the veteran who owns the house in effect ousting some other veteran. The veteran may not be occupying the house that he gives notice of eviction for, but undoubtedly it will result in the eviction of a substantial number of veterans.

I suggest to the committee that we leave the regulations as they are. I can assure the committee that the rentals administration and myself as minister are only too anxious to see that every relaxation is made which can be made fairly in the interests not only of the veterans but of all the people of Canada. Those relaxations will be made just as soon as we feel that can be done properly. Goodness knows it is no pleasure for the rentals administrator, and perhaps it is less pleasure for me as minister to have to resist what are undoubtedly deserving cases. Eviction control is a difficult and unpleasant thing to enforce, but I am satisfied the time has not yet come when we can do away with it.

As I said before, I am convinced that the suggested relaxation in favour of veterans who purchased their houses up to this time would not accomplish good for a considerable number of others; and I am satisfied that for the veterans themselves it would not be good.

,Liberal,,Douglas Charles Abbott,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4&Language=E&Section=ALL

1463130,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.13.1.11,1947-04-21,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. FLEMING:,,EMERGENCY POWERS,CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS,,Perhaps I might be

permitted to say something by way of clarification of the proposal. In the first place, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, in the statement he has read to the committee, has dealt in dark terms not only with the
Emergency Powers

present situation but also with the situation which might arise if my proposal were given effect to by the committee. Times have changed. Previously we have been treated to the most optimistic and expansive statements in the house about the great headway that the government, claimed was being made in the housing programme. Now, when a proposal is made with a view to bringing justice to veterans against whom, in effect, there has been discrimination, the picture is painted in dark colours. I mention this in passing, because it is a fact which may have to be referred to in the future.

I did not bring forward a proposal which would have the effect of increasing the difficulties of the problem. I brought before the committee two proposals, one of which was designed to give justice to veterans against whom discrimination does now exist. I coupled with that, ini the second place, a concrete proposal which would have the effect of greatly increasing the available supply of housing accommodation.

I was interested in hearing the indication given by the minister this afternoon of the high proportion of families occupying shared accommodation. That is most significant. Where families are occupying properties owned by veterans who under this proposal would be entitled to occupation of it, not only would there be provision for such persons in the increased supply of shared accommodation available under my second proposal, but there would be a great deal more of it.

The Minister of Finance suggests that more veterans may be hurt by this proposal than would be helped by it. I do not know where he gets his figures. It is perfectly clear that the proposal is confined] to cases where veterans are owners and desire the accommodation for their personal occupation. It does not touch at all veterans who are tenants of persons other than veterans. I submit that that would be the great proportion of veterans to whom the minister was referring when he spoke about the number of veterans who are tenants. The only such veterans who would be affected by this proposal are veterans who are tenants of veterans.

In these cases, obviously what the government ought now to be doing-or what it should be urging the wartime prices and trade board to do-is to bring about an extension of the effect of order in council P.C. 688. Surely before that order was made by the wartime prices and trade board, and before the government gave its approval to it, the situation must have been canvassed. That order bad the effect of opening the door to recovery of

possession by owners, regardless of whether they were veterans-and of course the great proportion were not-if they purchased the property between October 31, 1944 and July 25, 1945, the date of the freezing order.

In my humble submission the government took the measure which should have come second ahead of the measure which should have come first. They should have taken steps in the first place to put the veterans in at least as good a position-I would have said a preferred position-as that occupied by nonveteran owners. But surely the situation was canvassed at that time by the government to see that there was available a sufficient supply of housing accommodation to take care of any tenants who in the net result might have been dispossessed.

Something has been said to the effect that in view of the rate at which the number of families is increasing, the effect of dispossession is to lessen the total available housing accommodation per family. There may be something in that. It may be that in most cases veterans who are living in hovels, garrets or perhaps in a room or two, trying to keep their families together, but who have purchased houses and want possession of them for their personal use, would be living in larger quarters if they obtained possession of the places they have purchased. That is one reason why I have seen fit to put forward this constructive proposal with respect to freeing a great deal of housing accommodation which would be available today, on a shared basis, if it were not for the terms of the proposed order.

I come to the point raised by the Minister of Finance with reference to the terms upon which a landlord can recover possession of shared accommodation. He refers to the fact that possession can be recovered on six months' notice, but, Mr. Chairman, you know that that is not very helpful in inducing people to let one or two rooms in their house. The other provision for dispossession applies to a finding by the rentals board that the tenant is obnoxious. I do not need to emphasize again the extreme difficulty that is faced by a landlord in proving that a tenant is obnoxious within the terms of that rule. The terms of the order with reference to recovery by landlords of shared accommodation are so strict- and the minister must appreciate this-that they discourage many people from making available one or two or three rooms in their homes which are surplus to the needs of the occupant. It is an unquestioned fact, and it cannot be denied, that the order is discouraging people from renting shared accommoda-
Emergency Powers

tion. The occupants of homes who have more space than, they need simply will not take people into their homes because of the great difficulty of ridding themselves of the tenant if he proves difficult and unpleasant.

I quite agree with the observations of the Minister of Finance about the necessity of fixing a deadline for purchase by the veteran. I made it clear when I spoke on Friday last, and certainly in answer to questions of the Minister of Justice, that that was my proposal, that this provision should not be extended to cover future purchases of homes by veterans because of the danger of some of them making brokers of themselves. So there should be a deadline,
I suggest March 31, 1947. Then it would be quite clear that the period is closed now.

1463142,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.13.1.23,1947-04-21,4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4,ca.m.9666,Mr. ABBOTT:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,EMERGENCY POWERS,CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS,,I think that was in order 477. Security of tenure and the rental ceiling are closely linked in dwelling accommodation. The government fully realized the irksome character of the measure which was being enacted in granting security of tenure beyond the law of the province to a tenant who occupied an integral part of the landlord's own home and shared its facilities. Acting on that principle on October 1, 1943, we removed security of tenure from that type of accommodation. Well, the results were most unfortunate. As I stated1 a few moments ago, between twenty and forty per cent of the population of urban centres live in that type of accommodation, so that any untoward increase in the rental of the accommodation has a far-reaching effect. By the end of July, 1944, the board found as a result of freezing from security of tenure that type of accommodation that they had lost all control of the rental price of shared accommodation. Therefore board order 428 was enacted giving the tenants of such accommodation security of tenure terminable on six months' notice in the fashion I indicated a few moments ago.
There is no doubt that the heavy demand for dwelling space still continues and' still reaches down to the shared accommodation.

I know the hon. member for Eglinton will agree *with me in that; indeed he has already so indicated. Therefore there is no doubt that landlords fortunate enough to have available for renting shared accommodation which has not previously been rented, or which has

become vacant, would be able to demand and obtain far higher rental than the board would approve or has approved. I do not think there is any question as to that. But the new tenants, without security of tenure, would keep on, paying such excessive rentals as the tenants similarly situated did between October, 1943, and July, 1944. The landlords still saddled with tenants will be restive in their position of inferior advantage and will be seeking constantly to get their tenants out in order to take advantage of the admittedly illegal increase in revenue which the proposed amendment would permit. The resultant loss of control, disturbance and bickering makfes the suggestion most unattractive. Therefore on balance, as I said before, while the government is most anxious to remove control on these^ matters, the shortage of dwelling space remains so acute that our rental officials, who have had extensive experience in the administration of these orders, assure me that to attempt to remove security of tenure from this type of accommodation would make it impossible to continue to exercise any real control over the rentals. It is for that reason in particular that I am reluctant to consider such amendments as that put forward by my hon. friend1.

disadvantage if he did not; he should have. As I say, I wish to support the implication that the government is going too fast in the field of taking off subsidies.

The hon. member made reference to the resolution which passed this house last summer, to the effect that the milk subsidy should be retained. Of course it is history now that the government disregarded the views of the house and removed the subsidy, as soon as the house prorogued, or almost as soon as it prorogued. I shall not go into that because, as I say, it is history. But I think that is indicative of the way in which the government has been removing subsidies without taking into consideration the views of the house or of the people generally.

I want to give this illustration as an example of what happens if subsidies are taken off promiscuously, so to speak, without first viewing the whole picture. We had the announcement not so long ago that the price of binder twine, for example, is to jump approximately $7.50 a hundredweight. That, I understand, is the wholesale increase in the price, and it will work out somewhere in the neighbourhood of $9 a hundredweight by the time it comes to the farmer. It is quite true that in many cases in the west binder twine has gone out of vogue where combines: are now used; but in many parts of Canada, it is still a considerable item in the expense of the farmer during the harvest season. I do not know on what basis the government took the action which they did take in wiping out the subsidy and allowing this price increase. Surely there must have been some middle way, if they felt that the subsidy they were paying was too high or that the price was too low. There must have been some place in between where they were before and where they are now, where the government could have stopped. I cannot see any justification for the price of binder twine jumping $7.50 a hundredweight this year, and I think the government should reconsider its position in that regard and in many other instances along the same line. I could mention gasoline. I understand that part of the sub-

sidy is still being paid, while part has been removed, and that under decontrol the price of gasoline has gone up from two to two and a half cents in different provinces.

All those things enter into the cost of production of farm products, and the farmer has no alternative but to ask the government to decontrol the products he produces or, on the other hand, to absorb the difference himself. Before we leave this order in council dealing with the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, I believe the government should frankly place before parliament the policy they intend to follow in connection with the retention or removal of subsidies, so that the producers of this country whose products are still under price control, may have some idea of what it is going to cost them to continue production. The farmers of western Canada have been very patient, but that patience can be tried too far, as the government has reason to know from what happened last fall. I refer to the non-delivery strike, which lasted only a short time but was an indication of what could happen if the farmers of Canada actually went to work and put on a real non-delivery strike. We all hope that will not happen, and I am sure the farmers would be the last to want it to happen; but if they keep getting it from both ends, with prices of the things they are buying steadily creeping up, costs of production steadily increasing, and subsidies being withdrawn, with the farmer having to absorb the difference, I am not so sure that they will continue to take it. Therefore I trust the government will give us some real hope for this year, some reason to believe they will not rush along the path they followed last year in removing subsidies without regard to the effect on the producers.

1463244,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.14.17,1947-04-21,396d7d47-d79c-4aea-bf33-18c3e7b199e3,ca.m.9501,Mr. ILSLEY:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,UTISE) COITION,,,Naturally, when subsidies are imposed, it is difficult to withdraw them. There is immense opposition to the withdrawal of every subsidy, and a government that took the easy course, the path of least resistance, once they got into a jungle of subsidies, would I suppose, remain there forever. The views I have expressed with regard to subsidies have been something like this, that a subsidy policy at a time of grave danger of serious inflation is a valuable policy, in that it prevents the spiral of inflation from developing. If that spiral once gets under way it may carry prices to grave heights; and a judicious expenditure of government money by way of subsidy may result in a very much greater saving to the consumer in prices than the expenditure by way of subsidy. I gave an estimate of the amount which it might be argued had been saved in prices to consumers by the expendi-

ture of subsidies during the war years. But I believe there comes a time when the expenditure of government money in the way of subsidies becomes little or nothing more than a transfer of purchasing power from the taxpayers to the consumers. In the course of the payment of subsidies there comes a point when that becomes the case. When that time comes, then subsidies are not justifiable on the basis of prevention of uncontrolled or uncontrollable inflation at all. If they are to be justified it must be on another ground entirely; that is, that it is desirable to make a redistribution of purchasing power. That is always a debatable question.

As hon. members know, the taxation system of the country underwent a radical modification during the war. A much larger proportion of the revenues than had theretofore been the case was raised by direct taxation on the basis of ability to pay. This meant that persons in receipt of very low incomes paid no income tax; those in receipt of slightly higher incomes paid income tax at a low rate, and so on until in the higher brackets income taxes were imposed at a very high rate. That income tax being such a large proportion of the total tax, it meant that a redistribution of income was going on all the time under the taxation system. Just how far that redistribution of income and wealth should be supplemented by a subsidy policy is a difficult question./I think the general view of the government is that we should withdraw from subsidies as far as possible and as soon as possible, but that does not convey very much information to the members of the house, nor do I think the government can give any commitment with regard to the time when they withdraw from subsidies.

I would direct attention to two points in regard to that resolution. In the first place, it merely asked that consideration should be given the continuance of the milk subsidy. But,"" the chief executive went on, ""I must say in all frankness that the economic skies are not entirely clear. One cloud is shadowing our economic future.

If we are to avoid a recession we must act before it starts,"" he said.

First, like every other Canadian, he must live and must keep his family. So that when there is a general increase in prices his cost of living goes up. Secondly, with the general increase in the price of manufactured articles, his production costs rise. .

The farmer is most anxious about price controls. He believes his whole economic existence depends upon a fair relationship of his and other prices. Therefore he views with alarm a removal of subsidies and the consequent rise in prices.

This afternoon the minister said that, in his opinion, the wheat agreement could stand on its own feet. I believe that this agreement is sufficiently fair and in the right direction, so that it can stand on its own feet. But the price paid to the farmer by the wheat board is, in my opinion, not at this time sufficient to take care of the rapidly rising costs of production the farmer must pay. The farmer says, and I agree, ""We have accepted stable prices for a number of years. We like stable farm prices. But at the same time we want to have other prices stable, and we do not want our price for wheat frozen at $1.35 when, through government policy, the cost of production to the farmer is rising by leaps and bounds.""

Going across the country, I find that the people of the nation are fearful of a depression. The conversation usually goes like this. Someone you meet will say, ""We are experiencing inflation now, and in one or two years time we shall have a depression."" When you get the people of this country thinking there will be a depression, and they think so because we have inflation now, inevitably there will be a depression. The inflation we are now experiencing is the direct consequence of the government's removal of subsidies and its decontrol policy generally.

Last year many of the farmers in Saskatchewan and Alberta went on a non-delivery strike. In the area I know best, my own constituency, the farmers went on strike at a number of points. Often it was not where there were united farmers locals, but a spontaneous strike that developed as a result of a meeting of the farmers in the area deciding that they would not deliver their products. When you can have a farmers' strike of the magnitude of the one we had last year, then with the increasing costs of the things the farmer has to buy and frozen prices of wheat the government should realize that another non-delivery [DOT] strike may come about that will be supported by the farmers generally. tion. The impact of the war was more powerful in maintaining prices and wage controls than the law of the land because it strengthened the will of the nation to live and maintain its way of life.

What I object to is an argument from only one point of view. To maintain a really stable price control, you must control everything. Some hon. gentlemen maintain that we should have control in the industrial structure. That inevitably involves control of wages. Then you have the demand that costs of basic food products in this country should be controlled. That, by the very nature of things, means control of the farmer. Then you have the viewpoint that we should maintain subsidies and at the same time reduce taxes. But subsidies can come only from taxation. I still believe that two and two make four. It can be argued, according to the audience you are trying to impress, that two and two make five, but in this House of Commons, where we get all viewpoints, two and two still make four, and hon. gentlemen who are arguing for controls in one direction should be consistent and argue for the general control of everything. They should not argue both for subsidies to be continued and for taxation to be reduced.

What I think is necessary in this country today is self-discipline imposed as free men. Men and women in the industrial structure, using that word in its broadest sense and including those engaged in commerce, employers of labour and those engaged in manual toil in industry, have a responsibility to discipline themselves, and so have those who are engaged in the agricultural life of this nation. Unless we have that measure of selfdiscipline under our system of free institutions, we cannot face up to the problem my hon. friends often talk about. on the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, I wish to talk about the threatened increase in the price of butter, and the milk subsidy which this government withdrew. We have learned to our sorrow that when a rumour appears in the paper to the effect that rents are going up, that sugar is going up or that butter is going up, a few days later it becomes a fact. I think I should be remiss in my duty if I did not raise the point now in connection with the increase in the price of butter to the families of this country. I submit that the question is not control, subsidy or incentive. The question is, for whom are we to control and to wThom shall we pay the subsidy? I submit it is to him for whom the cash register rings, because

profits in this country have hit an all-time high, yet we have the gall to give subsidies to people like Crane Limited. That would be the equivalent of building a new pig pen on the farm of every farmer because we want more hogs, because his present pen is not big enough. Yet when we go to deal with the farmers, what do we do? We have the wheat contract for four years, but we are not taking one cent out of the treasury of Canada to cover our wheat contract. No. We add up the $1.55, plus $1.55, plus $1.55 for last year and the first two years of the contract, plus $1.25, plus $1 and we divide by five and get $1.35. So we say we will give an average price of $1.35 and it will not cost the Canadian people a cent. And we have, in effect, a price financed through the farmers' own contracts, not costing the Canadian people anything. We have, in effect, fixed for the next four years the return to the farmer from his wheat, which amounts to price control; and then we decontrol all his costs-his twine, his fertilizer, his fuel.

He also is a consumer. The farmer will buy a car; and heaven knows cars have gone up in price. I found to my sorrow that not only has the ten per cent gone on, but another $300 must be paid for itemized things which were never listed separately before. We bought a car just before Christmas and we thought we were to pay $1,500 and something for a little Plymouth; but when we went to take delivery we found another $300 and some odd listed-$25 for unloading, so much for servicing, so much for this and so much for that-and it cost us $1,800 and something by the time we took it out.

We buy cars and we buy salt; we buy sugar and we buy shoes. Yet we find that the government can control the price of leather. Oh, yes, we can control the price of leather, but we decontrol the manufactured shoe, so that the man who is making shoes gets the advantage of control in his costs and the double advantage of being able to decontrol when he sells you or me a pair of shoes. So I submit that through the whole Canadian economy the question is not control. It is, whom shall we control, what shall we control and for whom shall we control? If you go downtown and try to buy a shirt, you have great difficulty in doing so. I do not need to tell hon. gentlemen that. You have had a hectic time for two or three years. But I find we are subsidizing cotton yarn. According to the Minister of Finance at page 1939 of Hansard, ""a substantial subsidy is still being paid on raw cotton going into process.

I submit ia all seriousness that you dare not raise rents and take subsidies off milk and butter and in every way possible assist the people who have things for sale and enable them to reach an all-time high in profits at the expense of the man who is on a fixed wage or fixed income through long term contracts for the things he produces. I submit it will be a mistake if you continue to do this; and I believe you will in spite of everything we can say, because I think the manufacturer has the ear of the government to a far greater extent than has the housewife, the mother or the farmer. I notice that the stock of butter is up by millions of pounds over last year and yet, in spite of the fact that we have more butter, butter is to be sixty cents a pound. As I mentioned the other day, the whole experience of the United States has disproved the theory of this government that volume will decrease prices to the consumer. Volume has not decreased prices; it has merely accumulated profits; and if it brings on a depression, as it threatens to do, this government and this government only will be to blame.

1463359,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.14.132,1947-04-21,2db22441-d3ea-4e76-8d18-f4753949bd74,ca.m.812,Mr. BLACKMORE:,,UTISE) COITION,,,There must be a way out in a country which is as rich as Canada is. May I for a moment refer to the speech made by the Minister of Labour. The Minister of Labour has his own natural way of expressing himself, but he generally manages to hit the nail right on the head and1 face facts realistically. I think all hon. members will recall fairly well what he said: how in the world are you to have money for subsidies if you decrease taxation? I believe nearly every hon. member would like to see subsidies, such as the one on milk, retained. The remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle quite clearly indicated that she would like to see the subsidy on butter retained. Of course she would assume that prices of butter are being held up because of the desire on the part of certain people to make a profit. In the light of what she said, I should like to recall the remarks made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley

the other night as reported at page 2142 of Hansard. The hon. member quoted Dean Clement of the university of British Columbia, to the effect that last year butter fat cost 58'77 cents a pound to produce. He did not specify whether that was only in British Columbia; I presume it was, but he indicated quite clearly that he would veiy much like to know what would be the actual cost of the production of a pound of butter fat in Ontario. I believe, if all the hon. members of this house knew exactly what it cost in Ontario or in the maritimes or in any other part of Canada to produce a pound of butter fat, they would be greatly impressed. I believe we have been enjoying butter and a good many other things in Canada at a low cost for a long time, because the poor people who produce the butter and other things were simply absorbing part of the cost and producing at a loss. Now the time has come when, if we are to face the facts realistically and build for the future, we must cease calling upon any group of people to produce at less than cost.

The hon. member for Kamloops made some pertinent remarks, indicating that a number of producers whose raw products depended upon the activity of farmers had closed their doors because the farmers could no longer produce at the prices they were being offered, which prices were under their cost of production. We must face these facts. Merely talking about the difficulty will not solve the problem.

May I refer again to the remarks of the Minister of Labour. He said you just cannot have increased subsidies without increasing taxation. Let me say to the members of this house that when the minister made that remark he was wrong. That is one respect in which he just did not have the best information. Let me direct the attention of hon. members to this problem for a moment or two, and see how many can agree. The amount this country should be able to pay for butter ought to depend upon the milk, the apples, the potatoes, the lumber, the coal, the fish and all the other things Canada can produce. If Canada is able to produce a sufficient amount of all the other commodities the producer of butter needs, then certainly it is obvious that Canada should be able to pay that producer of butter enough of these various kinds of goods. Let us just face that set of facts squarely. If Canada is able to produce the goods of all kinds, to provide what is needed by the producer of any given commodity in order to enable him to make a living, then the time has come when this country must introduce a financial system under which it will be possible to pay that

individual the price he needs to receive. The fault lies in our financial system. We do not have a financial system which can reflect the facts of this country. So many of us do not look upon the wealth of Canada as the lumber, the coal and all the other goods and services we can produce. So many of us look upon wealth as the dollars and cents we can take or not take out of the pockets of the people of Canada. Which is a completely fallacious standard by which to judge wealth. I believe everyone in the country will agree that the wealth of this nation is the lumber, the coal, the fish, the food of all kinds, the clothing, the shelter and the other things this country can produce. If the country can produce enough wealth, then certainly we ought to be able to have the standard of living we desire, at least the standard which our production would justify us in enjoying.

That is the first important point. The very minute we recognize that, we shall not at all agree with the Minister of Labour. Then we shall recognize the fact that we might be able to pay greater subsidies without increasing taxation. I do not care a great deal about issuing challenges, but I should like to throw out a challenge to any member of this house to disprove the remark I made. I should like to see any member who thinks he can do so get up and disprove my statement, when I declare that the amount we should be able to pay for butter or any other commodity, or any kind of service in this country, should depend upon the milk, the cream, the cheese, the coal, the potatoes and the other goods we can produce in this country. If anyone can disprove that statement, we are ready to listen to him. I defy any man in this house to do so. I would be prepared to give him as many weeks as he needs to prepare his argument, and I would be ready to pick holes in that argument when he presented it here.

Now I should like to say just a few words in connection with subsidies. I believe, with the C.C.F., that the minister and the government as a whole are proceeding far too rapidly with the removal of subsidies. A good many people who have only half thought through the problems of this country are beginning to argue that we should remove subsidies; and the line of reasoning they are using is precisely the line used by the Minister of Labour, which was based on fallacy.

1463372,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.14.145,1947-04-21,2db22441-d3ea-4e76-8d18-f4753949bd74,ca.m.812,Mr. BLACKMORE:,,UTISE) COITION,,,May I for a few moments discuss the question of subsidies? I believe that subsidies should, be maintained and should be used definitely in Canada for an indefinite period of time, perhaps from now to the end. There are sound and fundamental reasons why that is so; and I particularly draw the attention, of the Progressive Conservative party to the problem I am going to present to them for a few minutes.

If they will take the Searle letter of April 17, 1947-and I think all hon. members received it-and turn to the last page, they will find an account of the Searle index which poses a serious problem to every person who bears a share of responsibility for the conduct of affairs in Canada. In the Searle index of things farmers bought, it is shown that the cost of 147 items now stands at 165-1 per cent, using the 1913-14 figure as 100 per cent. This means that those same things cost the farmers of the west today 65-1 per cent more than similar items of the same quality in 1913-14. Those costs have risen twenty-five per cent since August 1939. Hon. members might attribute the rise of twenty-five per cent since 1939 to the war. But they' cannot attribute to the war the other tremendous percentage increase, between 1913-14 and the outbreak of the war.

The index is quite clear that there is a general tendency- for prices to rise, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has pointed out so well. There is a general tendency for the price of manufactured articles to rise. And unless primary- products

oats, barley, wheat, milk and other things which the primary producer produces-are definitely subsidized, unless a floor is put under them, the tendency is for those prices to fall. In any- capitalistic economy, any free economy, any private enterprise economy, such as we have in Canada, and as they have in the United States, this produces a discrepancy- between the cost of secondary- products and prices of primary products. Both by statement and by clear implication the hon. member for Qu'Appelle pointed that out.

One of the problems which must face the government and the country from this time forward is how they can possibly bridge the gap between prices of secondary products and those of primary products. I submit in all sincerity that there is no way known to man whereby that can be bridged, except by subsidies.

There must be subsidies to bring down the prices of secondary products, and subsidies to bring up the prices of primary products, if the price structure of the country is to be on a parity- or to be what we call balanced. So that there is no escaping the conclusion that the subsidy- is here to stay, and must be used from this time forward.

It is one thing for President Truman to say that prices of commodities must come down. It will be an altogether different thing for him to tell how they are to come down. While I do not wish to offend my C.C.F. friends, I wish to say this definitely for their benefit, and for the benefit of those who think along similar lines, that for them to contend that the reason for the increase in manufactured goods prices is entirely the fact that private enterprise does our producing is for them to make a ghastly blunder. And if they go forward with that false notion they will simply be the blind leaders of people who will blindly follow.

Let us face these facts and devise a solution. We do not need to wait for another election. There is intelligence, honesty and honour enough in the house to discover a solution. Let us find it and apply it. But we shall not find it by blaming it on things which are not to blame; and free enterprise is not to blame.

The cause of the difficulty is mainly that there has been such a tremendous increase in the use of machinery. Then, there have been so many other factors entering into the price of things as they come off the factory assembly
Emergency Powers

line that the spread has been more or less automatic. I have not time to go into the matter in detail, nor do I think it would be in order to do so at this time. But any good textbook on economics will make the facts perfectly clear. To hon. members who wish to go into the matter with some care, I suggest that they read ""Controlling Depression"", written by Paul H. Douglas, Professor of Economics in the university of Chicago and published in 1935. This book is available in the library. It will explain the reasons for the price spreads clearly and give a possible solution. I say we must have subsidies in order to bridge the gap between the cost of secondary products and the price of primary products.

There is another matter, that of giving the consumer a chance. I am deeply sympathetic with the words of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. She appeals eloquently and inspiringly in the interests of the little people, the poor people, who have to buy and to live. We cannot allow prices to rise so that they will destroy these folk. I suppose every hon. member in the house has read the letter appearing in this evening's Ottawa Citizen addressed to the Minister of Finance and referring to $40 a week. Anyone who has not read it would do well to do so. Let him then go home and think seriously, realizing that the problem propounded in the letter is one which is facing people in the city of Ottawa right here, while we are in this chamber. And it is a problem which cannot be solved simply by talking.

Something must be done. Because of this rise in prices the people who are involved are suffering excruciating misery. We simply must take care of the consumers. So I say that when the government abolished the consumer subsidy on milk it committed a grave blunder, and set a precedent which could lead to many equally grave blunders.

It must be recognized that the consumers in Canada must be able to buy the goods the country produces. If they are not able to buy those goods they will fall into a state of semipoverty and misery, while the people who produce the goods will be short of markets. That, again, will be bad for Canada and will lead to unemployment.
So far as I can see, the consumer subsidy is the only device whereby we can be sure the consumers will have the purchasing power they need.

I believe that anything further I have in mind might better be said at a future time. However I join with those who have pleaded so earnestly for a cessation in the dangerous rise in prices. I should like to give the C.C.F.
full credit for the stand they have taken in this matter. They are entirely right. I do not agree with them in respect of technique, but only in this fact:
column2: Tonight they have advocated the payment of subsidies. I agree with them completely in that respect, but I do not think the subsidies ought to come from taxation, for taxation will destroy the incentive to produce. We might use a certain amount of taxation, but we must come to the point at which we shall create the means with which we shall pay the subsidy, and the means will be based upon the production this country is able to turn into the markets, and which it is capable of returning to the markets in increasing volume.

column1: This much having been said, I draw my remarks to a close.

from the Ottawa Citizen of this morning, and I intend to ask hon. members not to forget about it, because it is a challenge issued to a number of people who perhaps do not claim to be in the common people's class. Hon. members will find this letter interesting.

I am going to place it on Hansard, because I think it is a good example perhaps to the Minister of Justice or whoever may want to do away with subsidies and they may answer some of the questions and arguments raised in this letter. The letter is as follows:
$40 a Week Budget
Editor, Citizen:-This is an open letter to Finance Minister Abbott and the gentlemen who got the $2,000 tax-free money.

We are the gentlemen and one lady who received the $2,000 tax-free exemption. It is up to us to do a little bit for the fellow who did not have that privilege and who cannot come into this chamber and speak for himself. I, as one of the common people, am going to speak for them tonight, and I hope it will not fall on deaf ears. I continue with the letter:
The following cannot lightly he brushed aside -not turned off by saying the writer is an atheist or communist.

May I digress for a moment and say that the policies of this and other governments are responsible for the rising of the communist programmes in this and other countries. Do not blame the other fellow. The letter continues:

Our young people served in the war, returned home to the usual great promises, got married, spent their savings and gratuity on buildings and furniture at outrageous prices. Today they are faced by a situation which is the outcome of our system of government and which means trouble, want, and sorrow for these young people who after years of war hoped to build up a home and family here in Canada. How many of these young people are getting $40 per week? Can you Mr. Abbott show how a couple with even one child can live for less in Ottawa?
The following will give you some idea of what can be purchased for $40 per week:
63 meals per week at 30 cents....
(no extra meals for visitors)
Rent
50Doctor
50Newspaper
18Car fare
50Incidentals

Those items amount to $40, provided that a man can get a job at $40 a week and provided that he does not have sickness and some of the other difficulties which many people in the working class run up against. A little later on, he goes on to show that this amount provides nothing for shows, no tobacco or drinks, no entertaining, no holidays, no savings, no happiness, only worry. Then he asks: ""How does it look to you, gentlemen?"" It is signed ""E. Richardson, Ottawa.""

I have been on the production line of this country producing agricultural wealth for more than thirty years. I know the conditions that many of us have gone through, not because it was our fault but because it was the fault of governments in office. That same system prevails today. Some people give reasons of various kinds and I am going to give the committee one tonight. I expect to be challenged but, regardless of any argument that may be brought up, I think it will still hold good.

This is a little item which was given to me by a young lawyer friend in western Canada, in Lloydminster, in fact, a young man who spent some years in Ottawa during the war. He left here as a lieutenant-commander and is now practising law in Lloydminster. When speaking to me the other day he gave me this item. It illustrates perhaps some of the reasons why we have some of the mess in our country's government today. The article is as follows:
When a man gives you an orange, he simply says: ""Have an orange."" But when the transaction is entrusted to a lawyer, he adopts this form:

I hereby give and convey to you, all and singular, my estate and interests, right, title, claim and advantages of and in said orange, together with all its rind, juice, pulp and pips and all rights and advantages therein with full power to bite, cut, suck and otherwise to eat the same or give the same away with or without the rind, skin, juice, pulp and pipB, anything hereinbefore or hereinafter or in any other means or whatever nature or kind whatsoever to the contrary in any wise notwithstanding.""
Later on, another lawyer comes along and takes it away from you.

Perhaps some of the lawyers in the committee will tell us whether this is right. While this is considered a joke by many people, it is an expensive joke to the people of Canada. I think, if we got down to business and used some common sense instead of so much technicality in our money system we could have a commonsense system instead of the fallacious one we have used in the past, and then the people of Canada could enjoy the production of this land which could provide,

I have before me the national accounts, income and expenditure for the period 1938 to 1945. I find that the estimated distribution of income, recipients by income classes excluding agriculture and the armed forces, indicate that twenty per cent of our married men in the country received an income of SI,000 or less. That group of our people received 6-3 per cent of our national income. Let me repeat that. Twenty per cent of our wage earners received six per cent of the total income, while at the other end of the brackets three per cent of our people, with incomes of over 15,000, received fifteen per cent of the total national income. This suggests that the twenty per cent who get only six per cent of the national income are not able to protect themselves when prices rise. When the cost of milk goes up fifty per cent it means that they have to get along with less milk or butter

or go without dental treatment. Further, you find in the maritimes that thirty-eight per cent of the population received less than $1,000, and only thirteen per cent of the total income, while at the other end the two per cent who get over $5,000 get a total of fourteen per cent. In the wealthy province of Ontario you find only fourteen per cent of the people getting incomes of less than $1,000, and four per cent of the total income; but you have three per cent of the people getting over $5,000, who grab fifteen per cent of the total income. That was for the year 1942.

In a country like Canada, where you have a complete concentration of most of the major industries in the central part of the country, and most of the markets, since central Canada has the population, we find1 at the same time a flow of trade east and west, where practically everything that is produced has to be marketed in the central markets, so that in my opinion subsidies are necessary. ia paying the shot. In my opinion this question of subsidies lies at the root- of our economic problem. I do not think anyone can maintain price controls once that system of subsidies is removed; and I definitely believe that, if this economy is to survive under the present scheme of things, most of the basic industries in this country will have to be subsidized to some extent in order to hold down prices. 1463424,ca.proc.d.1947-04-21.14.197,1947-04-21,ba7c8691-5f1c-4bc4-9ec1-82c0a828db16,ca.m.1501,Mr. QUELCH:,,UTISE) COITION,,,In view of the remarks
made by the hon. member for Cape Breton [DOT] South, I rise to say a few words at this time.

I agree with him absolutely when he says that the prosperity of the nation in the future will depend to a large extent on the payment of subsidies, that is, under a system of private enterprise, in order to maintain the production of the country at its maximum level and to maintain the demand of the people against that production, there will have to be a system such as that referred to by the Minister of Veterans Affairs as a compensatory system. A compensatory system is described very well by Stuart Chase in his book ""Where will the Money Come From"" where he advocates subsidies in order to maintain the effective demand of the people. I have heard several ministers state that subsidies cannot be paid without maintaining price control or price ceilings. I would say that depends, first, upon the purpose of the subsidies; and, second, upon the condition of production at the time the subsidy is paid; that is to say, it will depend upon whether goods are scarce or whether goods are surplus. If goods are scarce, then you will have to maintain a price ceiling. If, on the other hand, your production is surplus, the subsidies can be paid without any price ceiling being maintained by rigid controls.

May I explain what I mean? During the war a very large percentage of our production was shipped overseas, with the result that the money paid out on that production became a demand against the production left in the country, and that purchasing power became a great stress upon the price structure within the country. The government therefore desired to prevent the prices of goods from rising, and for that purpose put into effect price control. In addition, in order to make it possible for industry to pay their costs under that price control, the government subsidized industries where the costs were greater than could be met under the price ceilings. If the government had merely said to the industries concerned, ""We will pay you a subsidy to make up for the increased costs, provided that you do not raise your prices,"" what would have been the result? In all probability some industries would have said, ""To heck with your subsidies. We will increase our prices to an extent greater than the subsidies. Therefore we will recover our cost plus a profit, to an extent we could not recover it under your subsidy."" In view of the fact that goods were so scarce at that time, after the subsidized goods had been sold the industries which had raised their prices would also have been able to sell their goods. That is why I say that when goods are scarce you will have to maintain price ceilings as well as subsidies.

What is to be the situation in the future? It will not be a question of reducing the demand against goods in short supply. The problem we shall face in future will be to increase the demand against expanding production, because we shall not be exporting fifty per cent of our production in the future and without bringing back imports in return. The total production of the country will be available to the people, plus the imports brought here in exchange for our exports. Just the other day Mr. Ruml issued a statement in which he said we shall probably have a depression on April 15, 1948. The analysis on which he based that statement is interesting. It supports 100 per cent the statement made by the governor of the Bank of Canada in 1946, to the effect that the great problem which will be facing this country in the near future will be lack of effective demand.

Mr. Ruml points out four reasons -why demand w'ill fall off at that time. He points out that today we have full employment. We have not quite full production because of strikes, etcetera, but we have a full demand against that production. The reason is that at the present time we are building up inventories. Those goods art not yet on the market, but the money paid out for building up those inventories is a demand against available production. In the second place, a large amount of money is being paid out for reconversion purposes; that is, to reconvert factories. That money is also a demand against available goods, because goods are not coming from those factories yet. Then he points out that at the present time a large proportion of our production is being exported with no goods being brought back in return under export credits. This means that money is being paid out in the production of goods that are not available for consumption in Canada; that is to say, the money paid out for the production
Emergency Powers

of goods which have been exported becomes a demand against the goods remaining. The fourth reason he points to is that today we still have a large amount .of savings built up during the war, which are a demand against out present production.

He points out that by 1948 the condition will be rapidly changing. Inventories will have been built up, and the goods will be coming on the market. Reconversion will be largely completed; the factories will be completed, and goods will be flowing from them. He points out that we cannot expect to continue to export goods abroad without bringing back imports in return, and that the savings carried over from the war will have been largely spent. Therefore he points out that by 1948 our production will be increasing in relation to demand; there will be a falling off of demand, so he prophesies that by April 15, 1948, people will say, ""This is not a recession; it is a depression."" He admits that very likely the government will take steps immediately to change that situation, and I am hoping that the government of this country will be prepared to do likewise. However the government knows very well that, once you allow a country to start on the road to depression it is not easy to stop it, because, once people lose confidence, it is very difficult to restore it.

So, Mr. Chairman, we have .suggested that it is possible to maintain demand through the use of subsidies, and that in order to maintain those subsidies it will not be necessary to have price ceilings. We say the government can meet with industry and say, ""If you are prepared to produce at a fair profit we will pay you a subsidy."" That is to say, the government will set up a commission whose duty it will be to examine the relationship between demand and supply from day to day, week to week and month to month. If over a period of three months, say, they find that demand is lagging behind supply at the rate of perhaps ten per cent, so that demand is only ninety per cent of supply, then through the commission the government would say to industry, ""We will pay you a subsidy of ten per cent on condition that you reduce your prices by ten per cent in order to restore the balance between demand and supply."" If any industry refused, obviously the industries that did agr.ee would be able to undersell the one that did not by ten per cent; and in view of the fact that the situation will not be the same as it was during the war, but one in which production is available, then an industry which refused to reduce its prices would have a great deal of difficulty in selling its goods in competition with goods which were being subsidized and sold at a lower price.

That is why I say in future, when production is expanding more rapidly than effective demand is being maintained, subsidies can be paid without the necessity of maintaining price control. It has been argued in this house that you cannot pay subsidies without increased taxation. During the war that was true; but the purpose in maintaining subsidies during the war was to maintain price control and thereby reduce the danger of inflation. Taxation also helped to reduce the danger of inflation; but now, after the war, it is necessary to take steps to safeguard the country against deflation, and the purpose of the subsidies would be to increase demand in relation to supply. The minister himself has said that at the present time the saving in subsidy will be no greater than the cost in taxation. Therefore, if you are going to try to increase the demand by subsidies, obviously you cannot pay for those subsidies by taxation, because you will not be increasing the demand in relation to supply but merely taxing people in order to pay the subsidies. When that situation develops; when we have to expand the purchasing power of the people in order to maintain demand against production, then obviously subsidies will have to be paid by national money, which, of course, will not be obtained by taxation.

I think that must be obvious, and that applies to the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops. Obviously he is still thinking of the situation that existed during the war, but that will not be the situation henceforth. The great problem we are going to face in this country will be the difficulty of maintaining an effective demand against our production. Before the war, we used to try to do that by maintaining a favourable balance of trade. It is generally recognized today, however, that if we want to have good relations with other countries in future we shall have to be prepared to accept the goods of other nations in return for our exports. Other nations will not be prepared to go into debt just in order that we may dump our unemployment problem on their doorstep. So I would suggest that in future, in order to maintain prosperity in this country, we can release the rigid price controls we have had in the past, maintain subsidies at the necessary level to maintain effective demand against our production, and finance those subsidies by national money.
